authors: Siahkouhi, M; Rashidi, M; Kang, WH; Bozorg, B
title: AI-assisted fibre optic sensing frameworks for automated monitoring of railway infrastructure
journal: JOURNAL OF INFRASTRUCTURE INTELLIGENCE AND RESILIENCE
abstract: This review examines the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) with fibre optic sensing (FOS) for automated structural health monitoring (SHM) of railway infrastructure, encompassing embankments, bridges, tracks, tunnels, and turnouts. Railways are among the most sustainable and strategically critical modes of transportation; however, their distributed nature, increasing axle loads, and harsh environmental conditions present significant monitoring challenges. Distributed fibre optic sensing (DFOS) systems, including fibre Bragg grating (FBG), distributed acoustic sensing (DAS), and Brillouin- and Rayleigh-based scattering sensors, are identified as uniquely capable platforms for real-time, long-range, and high-resolution measurement. Sensor deployment configuration, including gauge length, spatial resolution, and signal-to-noise ratio, critically determines whether a system supports train localisation or enables detection of track component defects such as fastener loosening, rail cracks, and ballast degradation. The convergence of AI with FOS has redefined SHM as a data-driven and predictive discipline. Machine learning algorithms including Q-Learning and Deep Q-Networks (DQN), deep learning architecture such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), and Gated Recurrent Units (GRU), and reinforcement learning (RL)-based frameworks enable automated defect detection, localisation, and maintenance optimisation. Emerging frameworks incorporating Large Language Models (LLMs) and Digital Twin (DT)-integrated RL offer new opportunities for adaptive, closed-loop decisionmaking in railway maintenance. This review systematically identifies principal deployment challenges, including sensor cross-sensitivity, signal attenuation, massive data volumes from DAS systems, environmental degradation of protective coatings, labour-intensive installation, high interrogator costs, and power constraints at remote trackside locations. Railway-specific resolutions and alternatives are presented for each challenge, grounded in current literature.

authors: Aryai, V; Abbassi, R; Abdussamie, N; Salehi, F; Garaniya, V; Asadnia, M; Baksh, AA; Penesis, I; Karampour, H; Draper, S; Magee, A; Keng, AK; Shearer, C; Sivandran, S; Yew, LK; Cook, D; Underwood, M; Martini, A; Heasman, K; Abrahams, J; Wang, CM
title: Reliability of multi-purpose offshore-facilities: Present status and future direction in Australia
abstract: Sustainable use of the ocean for food and energy production is an emerging area of research in different countries around the world. This goal is pursued by the Australian aquaculture, offshore engineering and renewable energy industries, research organisations and the government through the "Blue Economy Cooperative Research Centre". To address the challenges of offshore food and energy production, lever-aging the benefits of co-location, vertical integration, infrastructure and shared services, will be enabled through the development of novel Multi-Purpose Offshore-Platforms (MPOP). The structural integrity of the designed systems when being deployed in the harsh offshore environment is one of the main challenges in developing the MPOPs. Employing structural reliability analysis methods for assessing the structural safety of the novel aquaculture-MPOPs comes with different limitations. This review aims at shedding light on these limitations and discusses the current status and future directions for structural reliability analysis of a novel aquaculture-MPOP considering Australia's unique environment. To achieve this aim, challenges which exist at different stages of reliability assessment, from data collection and uncertainty quantification to load and structural modelling and reliability analysis implementation, are discussed. Furthermore, several solutions to these challenges are proposed based on the existing knowledge in other sectors, and particularly from the offshore oil and gas industry. Based on the identified gaps in the review process, potential areas for future research are introduced to enable a safer and more reliable operation of the MPOPs. authors: Sambhavi, YV; Angalaeswari, S; Palaniappan, R; Kumba, K; Ra, N; Vijayapriya, R
title: Hydrogen-powered electric vehicles: A state-of-the-art review
abstract: Hydrogen-powered electric vehicles have become a viable option for achieving sustainable, low-carbon transportation, especially for applications that require high utilization, quick refuelling, and long driving range. With a focus on proton exchange membrane fuel cells (FCs), hybrid powertrain architectures, and their integration into contemporary vehicle systems, this paper provides a thorough, up-to-date overview of hydrogen FC electric vehicle (HFCEV) technologies. FC technologies and system configurations, hydrogen generation pathways and related costs, and the operational features of FC battery and FC supercapacitor powertrains are all thoroughly reviewed in this study. In relation to hydrogen consumption, system efficiency, and durability, important elements of energy management and control approaches, such as rule-based, optimization-based, and artificial intelligence-driven strategies, are addressed. Additionally, the lifetime constraints and degradation mechanisms of automobile FC systems are also studied, highlighting the necessity of better materials and degradation-aware control algorithms to provide long-term operation. In contrast the international norms and safety considerations for other hydrogen storages and refuelling structured are also presented. A well-to-wheel and life cycle assessment studies are also considered for compare the environmental issues of the hydrogen based EVs with traditional and battery based EVs. In Indian circumstance, the assessment also observes modern controlling initiatives, deployment perspectives, and transportation applications across commercial, passenger, and heavyduty sectors. Subsequently, novel areas of study are described as critical facilitators of future hydrogen mobility, including low-platinum catalysts, advanced hydrogen storage technologies, digital twins, and artificial intelligence-based diagnostics. The results show that hydrogen-based electric vehicles can contribute significantly to sustainable transportation networks when supported by reliable infrastructure, renewable hydrogen generation, and ongoing improvements in FC durability and system integration.
